questions.prompt: Where does a click at row 1, column 2 place a token?

options.label: In that exact empty cell.
At the bottom of column 2.
In the next empty row-major cell.

questions.explanation: This 5×5 brief is click-to-place. Gravity belongs to the separate 6×7 challenge. A familiar game rule must not silently replace the actual requirement.

questions.prompt: What happens after a click on an occupied cell?

options.label: The board and current player stay unchanged.
The turn changes but the board does not.
The previous token is overwritten.

questions.explanation: A rejected move does not consume a turn. Returning the existing state preserves both ownership and board contents, making this invariant simple to test.

questions.prompt: Do four matching diagonal tokens win under the stated contract?

options.label: No; only horizontal and vertical runs count.
Yes; every familiar four-in-a-row rule applies.
Only if the board is full.

questions.explanation: The source names horizontal and vertical runs. Diagonal detection is a useful extension only after agreement; board fullness does not change the allowed directions.

questions.prompt: Why can a last-move check ignore other rows and columns?

options.label: A new winning line must include the only changed cell.
Every occupied cell is adjacent to the new token.
A winner can only appear on the outer border.

questions.explanation: The invariant is that the previous legal game state had no winner and exactly one cell changes. Any newly completed line therefore contains that cell.

questions.prompt: Does R R empty R R form a winning row?

options.label: No; the four tokens are not contiguous.
Yes; four matching tokens anywhere are enough.
Only when R plays next.

questions.explanation: The requirement is consecutive matching cells. Counting all tokens in a row without resetting at gaps incorrectly treats separated groups as one run.

questions.prompt: TypeScript: why use setGame(previous => move(previous, r, c))?

options.label: It computes the complete next game from the latest queued state.
It allows direct mutation of previous.
It prevents every future rerender.

questions.explanation: The functional update receives the current queued state and keeps turn, board, and winner together. It still requires immutable updates and does not suppress normal rendering.

questions.prompt: Python: why does copying only the outer list not make nested mutation safe?

options.label: The inner row lists are still shared.
Python lists cannot contain lists.
A shallow copy always deep-copies children.

questions.explanation: An outer copy creates a new container but retains row references. Copy the changed row as well, or build a new board, before writing the token.

questions.prompt: Put this baseline implementation recipe in dependency order. Each step prepares the next.

items.label: Place a token and check the result
Advance only a valid nonterminal turn

questions.explanation: First establish the input and state contract, then implement the dependent transformation, and finally validate the observable result. Reversing these steps risks testing a UI whose rules or input identity have not been defined. This order is a rehearsal recipe, not the only possible engineering workflow.
